title: Adrenal Disorders
path: Management of Clients with Problems of the Metabolic and Endocrine System
Conditions Affecting the Metabolic and Endocrine Systems

headings.title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Adrenal Glands
headings.content: The adrenal glands are vital endocrine glands located superior to each kidney, divided into two distinct anatomical regions: the outer adrenal cortex and the inner adrenal medulla. The adrenal cortex constitutes about 90 percent of the gland and is further subdivided into three zones, each producing specific steroid hormones essential for life. The outermost zona glomerulosa secretes mineralocorticoids, primarily aldosterone, which regulates sodium reabsorption, potassium excretion, and extracellular fluid volume. The middle zona fasciculata produces glucocorticoids, mainly cortisol, which is critical for carbohydrate metabolism, the stress response, immune suppression, and anti-inflammatory actions. The inner zona reticularis synthesizes adrenal androgens, such as dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), which contribute to secondary sexual characteristics. In contrast, the inner adrenal medulla is part of the sympathetic nervous system and consists of chromaffin cells that synthesize and secrete catecholamines, predominantly epinephrine and norepinephrine. These catecholamines mediate the rapid 'fight-or-flight' response by increasing heart rate, blood pressure, and blood glucose levels. Understanding this distinct zonation and hormonal output is foundational for nursing students, as dysfunction in any of these layers leads to severe fluid, electrolyte, and metabolic imbalances that require precise clinical intervention in Nigerian healthcare settings.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Classification of Adrenal Disorders
headings.content: Adrenal disorders broadly stem from either hypofunction or hyperfunction of the adrenal cortex or medulla. They are classically classified into primary, secondary, and tertiary etiologies. Primary disorders originate directly within the adrenal gland itself, such as destruction of the adrenal cortex leading to primary adrenal insufficiency or a tumor causing excess hormone secretion. Secondary disorders involve dysfunction of the pituitary gland, which fails to secrete adequate adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), thereby reducing stimulation of the adrenal cortex. Tertiary disorders involve pathology within the hypothalamus, characterized by deficient corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) production. Alternatively, hyperfunctional states can arise from hormone-secreting tumors, pituitary adenomas producing excessive ACTH, or ectopic ACTH production from non-endocrine malignancies like small cell lung cancer. Understanding these pathophysiological classifications helps nursing students trace the origin of clinical signs, anticipate diagnostic outcomes, and comprehend why replacement therapy differs fundamentally from suppressive medical therapy or surgical extirpation.

headings.title: Addison's Disease: Causes, Clinical Manifestations, and Crisis
headings.content: Addison's disease, or primary chronic adrenal insufficiency, results from the progressive destruction of the adrenal cortex, leading to a deficiency of both glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids. Common global causes include autoimmune destruction, while infectious causes like tuberculosis remain highly relevant in regions like Nigeria. Clinical manifestations develop insidiously and include chronic fatigue, progressive muscle weakness, weight loss, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, hypotension, and characteristic hyperpigmentation of the skin and mucous membranes due to elevated levels of melanocyte-stimulating hormone co-released with ACTH. The most life-threatening complication is an Addisonian crisis (acute adrenal insufficiency), typically triggered by acute stressors such as severe infection, trauma, surgery, or abrupt cessation of corticosteroid replacement therapy. An Addisonian crisis presents with profound hypotension, vascular collapse, dehydration, severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and hypoglycemia, constituting a true medical emergency requiring immediate intravenous fluid resuscitation, high-dose glucocorticoid administration, and intensive nursing monitoring.

headings.title: Cushing's Syndrome and Cushing's Disease
headings.content: Cushing's syndrome refers to the clinical condition resulting from chronic exposure to excessive circulating levels of glucocorticoids. When this syndrome is specifically caused by an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma, it is termed Cushing's disease. Other causes include adrenal adenomas or carcinomas secreting excess cortisol autonomously, or ectopic ACTH production from non-pituitary tumors. Clinical manifestations are distinct and include central or truncal obesity with a characteristic 'moon face' and 'buffalo hump,' muscle wasting in the extremities, thin and fragile skin easily bruised, purple abdominal striae, osteoporosis, hypertension, secondary diabetes mellitus due to induced insulin resistance, and emotional lability ranging from depression to psychosis. In clinical practice, nurses must carefully observe patients for signs of fluid overload, hyperglycemia, and increased susceptibility to opportunistic infections due to steroid-induced immunosuppression. Early recognition and targeted intervention are vital to prevent long-term systemic complications.

headings.title: Pheochromocytoma: Recognition and Acute Presentation
headings.content: Pheochromocytoma is a rare, catecholamine-secreting tumor that originates from chromaffin cells, most commonly located within the adrenal medulla. These tumors autonomously and episodically secrete massive amounts of epinephrine and norepinephrine, leading to a dangerous triad of classic symptoms: severe episodic headaches, profuse diaphoresis, and tachycardia accompanied by severe paroxysmal hypertension. Acute presentations can be life-threatening, precipitating hypertensive emergencies, acute myocardial infarction, cerebrovascular accidents, or fatal cardiac arrhythmias. Nurses must recognize that routine activities, physical stress, abdominal palpation, or certain medications can trigger these severe hypertensive attacks. Diagnostic workup involves measuring urinary and plasma fractionated metanephrines. Preoperative management requires careful medical stabilization using alpha-adrenergic blockers first, followed by beta-blockers, to control blood pressure and expand intravascular volume before any surgical manipulation is attempted, thereby preventing catastrophic intraoperative hypertensive crises.

headings.title: Diagnostic Evaluation and Laboratory Findings
headings.content: Accurate diagnosis of adrenal disorders requires a systematic combination of biochemical testing, provocative stimulation tests, suppression tests, and advanced radiological imaging. For suspected adrenal insufficiency, the short cosyntropin (ACTH) stimulation test is the gold standard, where synthetic ACTH is administered and cortisol levels are measured; a failure of cortisol to rise indicates primary or secondary insufficiency. Conversely, for Cushing's syndrome, screening involves the 24-hour urinary free cortisol test, late-night salivary cortisol assays, or the overnight dexamethasone suppression test, which evaluates whether cortisol secretion can be normally suppressed. Plasma and urinary metanephrines are tested to diagnose pheochromocytoma. Once biochemical abnormalities are established, radiological studies such as computed tomography (CT) scans or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the adrenal glands and pituitary gland are utilized to locate tumors or assess glandular size. Nursing responsibilities include patient preparation, scheduling tests accurately, ensuring proper sample collection, and managing patient anxiety throughout the diagnostic evaluation.

headings.title: Medical and Surgical Management
headings.content: Medical and surgical management of adrenal disorders depends entirely on the specific underlying pathology and whether the gland is hyperfunctional or hypofunctional. For primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease), lifelong hormone replacement therapy is mandatory, consisting of oral glucocorticoids (such as hydrocortisone or prednisone) and mineralocorticoids (such as fludrocortisone), with dosage adjustments during periods of physical illness or stress. Hyperfunctional states like Cushing's syndrome and pheochromocytoma typically require surgical intervention, such as a unilateral or bilateral adrenalectomy, or transsphenoidal removal of a pituitary adenoma in Cushing's disease. Medical therapy may also be used preoperatively or for inoperable tumors to block steroid synthesis (e.g., ketoconazole, metyrapone) or manage symptoms. Surgical approaches carry risks of hemorrhage, infection, and temporary or permanent adrenal insufficiency, necessitating meticulous postoperative care, hemodynamic monitoring, and prompt initiation of replacement corticosteroids to prevent acute crisis.

headings.title: Nursing Care Plan and Patient Education in the Nigerian Clinical Context
headings.content: In the Nigerian clinical context, caring for patients with adrenal disorders presents unique nursing challenges due to resource limitations, prevalent infectious etiologies like tuberculosis, and economic constraints affecting long-term drug adherence. The nursing care plan must focus on monitoring vital signs, managing fluid and electrolyte imbalances, preventing infection, and providing comprehensive patient and family education. Nurses must emphasize the critical importance of lifelong medication adherence for patients with Addison's disease, teaching them never to abruptly stop their steroid medications. Patients and their caregivers must be educated on sick-day rules, which involve doubling or tripling oral steroid doses during minor illnesses and recognizing early signs of an Addisonian crisis so they can seek immediate healthcare facility presentation. For postoperative adrenal surgery patients, nursing care involves strict monitoring of blood pressure, managing surgical site incisions, and observing for signs of acute adrenal crisis. Culturally sensitive health education delivered in local languages ensures better understanding, compliance, and improved health outcomes across diverse Nigerian populations.
